overview: The CC Planning and Permitting committee manages the modernization and overhaul of the city's zoning ordinances and land use regulations. Its primary responsibilities include refining zoning definitions, creating new corridor-specific districts, and establishing development standards for residential and commercial growth. The body began its work in May 2024 by prioritizing technical updates and has since moved through neighborhood-by-neighborhood rezoning efforts. As of May 2026, the committee has most recently referred a major rezoning proposal for the Boston Avenue corridor and Tufts University area for joint review with the Community Development Board.

threads.name: Comprehensive Zoning Modernization
threads.summary: The committee initiated a multi-year project to digitize the zoning map and modernize the table of uses and definitions to resolve regulatory gaps and non-conformities identified by city staff. Early work focused on non-substantive formatting changes and neutral definitions for residential types, eventually leading to the referral of a foundational zoning package in May 2024. Later sessions addressed technical cleanup of procedural language and the alignment of local codes with state mandates. Ongoing work includes mapping analysis and periodic technical updates to ensure citywide consistency across new sub-districts.

threads.name: Mystic Avenue Corridor Rezoning
threads.summary: Beginning in mid-2024, the committee focused on transforming the auto-oriented Mystic Avenue into a walkable mixed-use corridor. Proposals introduced tiered building heights ranging from six to twelve stories and 'curb setbacks' to facilitate wider sidewalks on private property. The committee approved a specific model using incentive zoning to trade increased height for community benefits. The final proposal, which established four new sub-districts, was referred to the full City Council in October 2024.

threads.name: Salem Street Corridor Rezoning
threads.summary: The committee reviewed zoning for the Salem Street corridor to establish density nodes at major intersections while preserving existing residential blocks. Discussion centered on the feasibility of four-to-six-story building heights on small parcels and the use of step-backs to minimize visual impact on the narrow streetscape. In December 2024, the body referred a plan to the City Council that legalized existing non-conforming commercial uses and introduced height bonuses for projects providing deeper affordability and public parking.

threads.name: Neighborhood and Urban Residential Zoning
threads.summary: The committee worked to replace single-family zoning with a density gradient across five new sub-districts, ranging from low-density neighborhoods to transit-oriented urban zones. Initial drafts were scaled back to protect the character of single-family areas while formalizing small-scale 'neighborhood nodes' for local businesses. Special attention was paid to ensuring that existing non-conforming homes could be renovated without requiring variances. The committee referred the completed residential zoning proposal in February 2025.

threads.name: Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs)
threads.summary: To comply with new state mandates, the committee developed a local ordinance governing Accessory Dwelling Units. Members debated discretionary regulations such as setback requirements, height limits for detached units, and a ban on short-term rentals. The body also established special permit requirements for properties seeking to add a second ADU or utilize historic accessory structures. The final set of ADU regulations was referred favorably in April 2025.

threads.name: Environmental and Green Score Standards
threads.summary: In September 2024, the committee reached a consensus to implement a 'green score' metric to mitigate urban heat and manage landscapes for projects triggering site plan review. This 100-point rubric was referred as a standalone ordinance in November 2024 to ensure environmental performance standards for new developments. The committee has continued to integrate these standards into corridor-specific plans, recently increasing the score requirements for the Boston Avenue corridor to 25 points to encourage more substantial green infrastructure.

threads.name: Tufts Institutional Zone and Boston Avenue
threads.summary: The committee developed a new institutional zoning district to better manage Tufts University's expansion and clarify the jurisdictional reach of the Dover Amendment. Early discussions explored how to regulate campus buildings that were previously categorized under residential zoning and how to create sub-areas that face residential neighborhoods. In May 2026, the committee referred an amended plan that includes three mixed-use sub-districts along Boston Avenue, specifically prohibiting drive-through restaurants and gas stations while setting incentive-based height limits.

threads.name: Medford and West Medford Squares
threads.summary: Zoning for the city's commercial squares was updated to increase residential density near transit hubs. For Medford Square, the committee established 'daylight standards' and angular planes to protect sunlight for abutting homes, while West Medford Square was rezoned to incentivize housing near the commuter rail. Both square proposals were referred to the Community Development Board in April 2025. By 2026, the city also began exploring 40R 'Smart Growth' overlays for Medford Square to unlock state funding for the high school project.

threads.name: Vacant Property and Rental Protections
threads.summary: The committee initiated legislation to address commercial vacancy and tenant displacement. This included a draft condominium conversion ordinance featuring relocation payments and a review board to protect rental stock. Additionally, the body is refining a vacant building ordinance that would establish an escalating fee structure and a registry for empty commercial properties to encourage reinvestment. Both items remain under legal and staff review as of early 2026.
